# 

# Tech-selection study

# Case study: network 230

![][image1]

Case study is a low-voltage network in Sion/Sierre that hosts a total base-load of 27 kW (considering 6% of nominal fuse rating and power factor of 0.9) and is served by a 400 kVA transformer. Under the SFOE scenario of 2040, the network is projected to host a total PV installation of 87 kWp and 11 electric vehicles.

![][image2]

# Horizon: a Day (15-minutes time-step)

##  only base loads

#### ![][image3]

Considering  only the base load and generating a daily profile using Inhouse profile generator (Grammatikos, et.al.) , nodal voltage are within operational bounds (+-1 p.u) and line currents are within the amperage ratings of the lines. This verifies the sanity check carried out on the low-voltage networks, because for a healthy network, as a gross error detection, should have no operational violations considering in its current state. 

## Base loads \+ PV generation

Pvlib was used to convert irradiance data into normalized DC power (via the haydavies/ineichen/faiman models), for two weather scenarios — an idealized clear-sky simulation ("clearsky") and PVGIS-TMY typical-year weather ("measured"). 

To generate one day profile representative of the year, we select the day with minimum RMSE from the average day of the yearly profile.

The considered PV generation profile results line amperage ratings violation in one line

To verify the hypothesis that substandard ESS selection occurs only in scenario where ESS solution required must be mostly in charging mode (e.g., problem violations that arise from PV over-generation), lets give them the same C-rate 1.1 and compare the investment cost alone:  
Li \- Ion :  28.447  
Na-Ion:  29.3663

This gives strong backing to the hypothesis;

## Base loads + PV + EV generation

Same network, same day-horizon (15-minute time-step), PV series \= clearsky, PV factor \= 1 (no scaling). Demand and EV realizations are identical to the base-loads+EV section above (same network, same rng seed, demand generated before PV/EV in the pipeline, so the profile axis doesn't perturb it).

### Operational violations

Combining PV export and EV charging load on top of the base loads produces both failure modes seen separately in the sections above: 12 nodes see undervoltage (Vmag0 down to 0.856 p.u., below the 0.9 p.u. floor) across 192 (node, timestep) instances, and one line (line 22\) sees a severe over-current, peaking at 261% of ampacity, across 32 timesteps.

### Tech selection, three cost functions × three technology scenarios

All three scenarios (Li-Ion only / Na-Ion only / Both) site ESS at the same three nodes as the base-loads+EV case: 34, 35, 41\.

With the throughput-loss penalty active, per-node throughput at node 34 collapses (39.5→7.6 kWh for Li-Ion-only, 47.1→7.2 for Na-Ion-only) while nodes 35/41 barely move — node 34 was doing the most "wasteful" cycling under F^inv+F^Sloss, and the penalty specifically suppresses that, not overall dispatch. **Na-Ion again loses its F^inv/F^inv+Sloss advantage once losses are priced**: total cost for Na-Ion-only (45.540 kCHF) now exceeds Li-Ion-only (42.112 kCHF) — the reverse of every earlier ranking in this section — consistent with the EV-only section's finding that Na-Ion's efficiency disadvantage only shows up once F^Eloss is actually priced. Both still wins overall (39.151 kCHF), letting the solver put Na-Ion only where its C-rate genuinely pays off (node 34, the lowest-throughput site) and Li-Ion where cycling is heavier (35, 41).

### C-rate-equalized check: is Na-Ion still "wasting energy" at C-rate 1.1?

Same test as the EV-only section's hypothesis check, repeated here for base loads \+ PV \+ EV, and extended to the loss-priced objective — since "wasting energy" is specifically the F^Eloss story, checking F^inv alone isn't enough to settle it:

| Cost function | Li-Ion (kCHF) | Na-Ion, C-rate forced to 1.1 (kCHF) | Gap |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| F^inv | 28.434 | 29.353 | \+0.919 |
| F^inv \+ F^Sloss \+ F^Eloss | 42.112 | 48.823 | \+6.711 |

At matched C-rate, Na-Ion loses on investment cost alone (28.434 vs 29.353 kCHF) — same direction as the EV-only section's original result (28.447 vs 29.3663) — confirming Na-Ion's real (C-rate=5) F^inv advantage seen earlier in this section (26.256 vs Li-Ion's 28.434) genuinely comes from the C-rate difference, not from the solver exploiting something for free.

**Yes, Na-Ion is still "wasting energy" at equal C-rate — more clearly than before.** Once F^Eloss is priced, the gap at matched C-rate widens more than 7× (0.919 → 6.711 kCHF), far more than F^inv alone would suggest. With C-rate no longer available as an offsetting advantage, Na-Ion's worse round-trip efficiency (0.85 vs 0.90) shows up directly as extra required energy capacity at the harder-worked nodes (35: 44.1→46.7 kWh, 41: 7.84→8.30 kWh under F^inv; node 34 is untouched, 13.6 kWh either technology) and gets punished sharply once that extra cycling is actually costed.
